lesson.intro:
Berlin does not do subtle weather. November arrives as a wall of grey drizzle, the sun clocks off before you have finished lunch, and by January the bridges over the Spree are quietly icing over while the road either side of them is merely wet. Add wet tram rails (*Straßenbahnschienen*) in Friedrichshain, a carpet of soaked lime leaves in the Tiergarten and a cyclist in a black hoodie on an unlit bike lane, and you have the theory exam's favourite playground: **the driver who did everything legally and still could not stop in time**.

This module covers the two halves of bad conditions: *being seen*, which means knowing exactly which switch does what and which one is a trap, and *staying in control*, which means aquaplaning, black ice, wildlife and glare. Learn the numbers here. The exam adores the fog lights, and it adores them precisely because almost everybody gets them wrong.

sections.heading: Which light, and when
sections.body:
German lighting law is refreshingly blunt. During twilight (*Dämmerung*), in darkness, or whenever the visibility conditions otherwise require it, you must use the prescribed lighting, which in practice means **dipped beam** (*Abblendlicht*). There is no calendar date and no clock time attached: the trigger is the light and the weather, so a black thunderstorm at two in the afternoon switches your headlights on just as reliably as sunset does.

Two traps live inside that innocent little rule.

- **Daytime running lights** (*Tagfahrlicht*) are not headlights. They exist to make you visible from the front on a bright day. They do not light the road, and on many cars the tail lights stay dark, so the driver closing on you through the spray sees precisely nothing. Where fog, snowfall or rain significantly impair visibility, the law wants dipped beam, not daytime running lights.
- **Position lights alone** (*Begrenzungsleuchten*, colloquially *Standlicht*) belong to a parked car, not a moving one. Driving on them is expressly forbidden.

When the car is standing still the rules relax. Outside built-up areas a parked vehicle must be marked by its **own** light. Inside a built-up area it is enough to mark the side facing the carriageway with parking lights, and if the street lighting already makes the car clearly visible, you need no light of your own at all, which is why most parked cars in Berlin sit there entirely dark and entirely legally. Vehicles over 3.5 t (other than cars) and trailers are the exception: standing **on the carriageway** inside a built-up area, they must always be marked by their own light source or another approved lighting device, however good the street lighting is.

Keep the lenses clean while you are at it. Lighting equipment that is covered or filthy counts as lighting you do not have, and a Berlin winter paints a headlight with grey salt film in about two days.

callout.text: Dipped beam is mandatory during twilight, in darkness, and whenever fog, snowfall or rain significantly impair visibility, even at midday (StVO §17(1), §17(3)).

sections.heading: High beam manners

callout.text: Not dipping in time for oncoming or preceding traffic: €20 (€25 if you endanger someone, €35 if it causes a crash). High beam on a continuously lit street, or driving on position lights alone: €10. Misusing the Lichthupe or the horn so that it harasses somebody: €10.

sections.heading: Fog: the tale of two 50s
sections.body:
Fog hands you two separate switches with two completely different rules, and confusing them is the most reliable trap in this whole topic.

**Front fog lamps** (*Nebelscheinwerfer*) may be used when fog, snowfall or rain **significantly impair visibility**. That is the whole condition: no metre threshold, and rain and snowfall both count. In that weather two fog lamps together with the position lights may even be used instead of dipped beam.

**The rear fog lamp** (*Nebelschlussleuchte*) is far stricter. It may only be switched on **when fog reduces visibility to less than 50 m**. Not rain. Not snowfall. Not "it looks a bit murky". Fog, under 50 metres. It is savagely bright by design, and left on in clearer air it blinds the driver behind you and drowns out your brake lights.

Now the elegant consequence the exam wants you to spot: if visibility is under 50 m, you are capped at **50 km/h** anyway, on every road, motorway included, whatever the signs say. So the rear fog lamp and 50 km/h always travel as a pair. A rear fog lamp glowing at 90 km/h is a contradiction in terms.

How do you judge 50 m inside the soup? Outside built-up areas the reflective guide posts (*Leitpfosten*) along the verge are normally spaced about 50 m apart on straight sections. Spacing tightens on bends, so treat it as a hint rather than a ruler. If you can still just make out the next post, you have roughly 50 m. If it has dissolved, you do not.

callout.text: Nebelschlussleuchte: fog only, visibility below 50 m only, and then never faster than 50 km/h. Switching it on in better conditions costs €20, and dazzles everyone behind you.

sections.heading: Aquaplaning: when the tyres go surfing

callout.text: Aquaplaning drill: off the gas, wheel straight, no braking, no steering. Then reduce speed properly before the next stretch of standing water.

sections.heading: Ice, frost and wet leaves
sections.body:
Cold does not arrive evenly. Certain places freeze while the rest of the road is merely wet, and the exam expects you to know them:

- **Bridges and overpasses**: cold air below as well as above, so they ice up first and thaw last.
- **Shaded stretches**: the north side of tall buildings, cuttings, and roads through woodland such as the run out towards Grunewald.
- **Dips, hollows and roads beside water**, where damp cold air settles.

**Black ice** (*Glatteis*) needs no deep freeze. A road surface chilled below zero plus rain, drizzle or thawing moisture is quite enough, so it can catch you with the air thermometer sitting around zero, classically at dawn after a mild night. Treat the first cold morning of the season as an ice morning until proven otherwise, and remember that it may cover only thirty metres of one bridge.

Autumn runs its own edition. **Wet leaves** (*nasses Laub*) act like a lubricant and hide whatever is underneath; so do wet **cobbles** (*Kopfsteinpflaster*), painted road markings and, very Berlin, wet **tram rails**. Cross rails at as open an angle as you safely can, never brake or steer hard while your tyres are on the steel, and leave cyclists plenty of room, because rails put them on the ground far more often than they trouble cars.

Germany's winter tyre requirement is **situational**, not calendar-based: on black ice, packed snow, slush or frost you must be on winter tyres. Since 1 October 2024 only tyres carrying the **Alpine symbol** (three peaks with a snowflake) satisfy it. An M+S marking on its own no longer counts.

callout.text: Driving in wintry road conditions without Alpine-symbol winter tyres: €60 and 1 point, and more if you obstruct or endanger others.

sections.heading: Wildlife, glare and reading the road ahead

callout.text: Animal on the road: brake, hold the wheel, stay in your lane. Never swerve into oncoming traffic to save an animal.

key_takeaways: Dipped beam during twilight, in darkness, and whenever fog, snow or rain significantly cut visibility, midday included.
Daytime running lights light nothing behind you, and you may never drive on position lights alone.
Dip the high beam for oncoming traffic, for vehicles you are following, and on continuously well-lit streets, then slow down too.
Front fog lamps: allowed in significant visibility impairment from fog, snowfall or rain. No metre limit.
Rear fog lamp: fog only, visibility under 50 m only, and then never faster than 50 km/h.
Aquaplaning: off the gas, wheel straight, no braking, no steering inputs, then slow down properly.
Bridges, shaded stretches and woodland freeze first; wet leaves, cobbles and tram rails quietly steal grip.
Animal ahead: brake hard, hold the wheel, high beam off, horn on, and never swerve.

german_terms.en: duty to drive slowly enough to stop within the distance you can see

questions.text: When must you switch on your vehicle's prescribed lighting?

options.text: During twilight and in darkness
Whenever fog, snowfall or rain significantly impair visibility, even in the middle of the day
Only between 1 October and 31 March

questions.explanation: The law ties lighting to conditions, not to the calendar or the clock. You must use the prescribed lighting during twilight (Dämmerung), in darkness, or whenever the visibility conditions otherwise require it, and dipped beam is separately mandatory whenever fog, snowfall or rain significantly impair visibility, which can easily happen at two in the afternoon. Germany has no seasonal lighting period.

questions.text: Heavy rain has cut visibility right down on the A100. Why are your daytime running lights not enough?

options.text: Daytime running lights only make you visible from the front by day; they do not light the road, and on many cars the tail lights stay dark
Where fog, snowfall or rain significantly impair visibility, the law requires dipped beam
Daytime running lights are brighter than dipped beam and therefore illuminate the road ahead better

questions.explanation: Daytime running lights (Tagfahrlicht) were designed for one job: making a car conspicuous from the front on a bright day. They throw no useful light onto the road, and on many vehicles they leave the rear lights switched off, so in spray the driver approaching from behind sees nothing at all. Once fog, snowfall or rain significantly impair visibility, dipped beam (Abblendlicht) is legally required, and that also brings your tail lights on.

questions.text: In which situations must you switch off or dip your high beam?

options.text: When a vehicle is coming towards you
When you are following another vehicle at close distance
When you are driving on a street with continuous, adequate lighting

questions.explanation: All three are genuine dipping duties. You must dip in good time for oncoming traffic and for a vehicle you are following closely, because your beam reflects out of their mirrors and blinds them just as effectively as it would head-on. High beam is also forbidden on roads with continuous, adequate lighting. Note the precise criterion: it is the continuous lighting, not merely being inside the town sign, so an unlit residential lane within a built-up area may still be driven on high beam until somebody appears.

questions.text: When may you use your front fog lamps (Nebelscheinwerfer)?

options.text: When fog, snowfall or rain significantly impair visibility
At any time in darkness, because they show the kerb more clearly
Only once visibility has dropped below 50 m

questions.explanation: Front fog lamps are tied to the weather, not to a measured distance: they may be used when fog, snowfall or rain significantly impair visibility. In that weather two fog lamps together with the position lights may even be used instead of dipped beam. They are not general-purpose night lights, and the 50 m threshold belongs to the rear fog lamp, so do not transplant it onto the front ones.

questions.text: When may you switch on the rear fog lamp (Nebelschlussleuchte)?

options.text: Only when fog reduces visibility to less than 50 m
Also in torrential rain or dense snowfall, as soon as visibility falls below 50 m
On every motorway journey after dark, so that you are easier to see

questions.explanation: This is the classic exam trap, and the rule is deliberately narrow: the rear fog lamp may only be used when *fog* reduces visibility to less than 50 m. Rain and snowfall permit the front fog lamps but never the rear one. The reason is glare: the rear fog lamp is far brighter than a normal tail light, so in clearer conditions it dazzles the driver behind and makes your brake lights almost impossible to pick out.

questions.text: Fog has reduced your visibility to about 40 m on a rural road. What is the maximum speed you may drive, in km/h?
questions.explanation: Once fog, snowfall or rain bring visibility below 50 m, a hard legal ceiling of 50 km/h applies on every kind of road, motorway included, and regardless of any higher signposted limit. It can be lower still if conditions demand it, because the underlying duty is always to drive slowly enough to stop within the distance you can actually see (Sichtfahrgebot).

questions.text: You have just switched your rear fog lamp on. What follows from that?

options.text: Your speed must not exceed 50 km/h, because visibility is below 50 m
You must switch it off again as soon as visibility improves, so as not to dazzle the drivers behind you
You may leave it on for the rest of the trip, since extra visibility can only help

questions.explanation: The two 50s are linked. If you are legally entitled to use the rear fog lamp, then fog has cut visibility below 50 m, and below 50 m visibility your maximum speed is 50 km/h. So a rear fog lamp glowing at motorway speed is a self-contradiction. As soon as the fog thins the entitlement disappears and the lamp must go off: leaving it on dazzles following traffic and swamps your brake lights, and it costs €20 (€25 if you endanger someone, €35 if it leads to a crash).

questions.text: You pass the town exit sign onto an unlit country road at night, driving on dipped beam. How fast may you go?

options.text: Only so fast that you can stop within the distance you can actually see
On dipped beam that will often mean clearly less than 100 km/h
The default limit outside built-up areas is always safe, whatever the visibility

questions.explanation: A speed limit is a ceiling, never a permission. The Sichtfahrgebot requires you to drive slowly enough to stop inside the stretch of road you can see, so your view, not the sign, sets your real maximum. Dipped beam lights only a few dozen metres of road, which on an unlit rural road puts the lawful speed well below the 100 km/h default. Driving faster than your own headlights reach is called overdriving your lights, and it is a leading cause of night-time collisions with cyclists, pedestrians and stationary obstacles. One narrow exception exists, and only on the Autobahn: there you need not match your speed to the reach of your dipped beam if the tail lights of the vehicle ahead are clearly visible and you keep a sufficient distance, or if reflector guide posts show the line of the road and other light reveals obstacles in time.

questions.text: Which statements about lights on a stationary or parked vehicle at night are correct?

options.text: Outside built-up areas a parked vehicle must be marked by its own light
Inside a built-up area no light of your own is needed if the street lighting makes the vehicle clearly visible
You may drive short distances on position lights (Standlicht) alone

questions.explanation: Outside built-up areas a stationary vehicle has to be made visible by its own light source. Inside a built-up area it is enough to mark the side facing the carriageway with parking lights, and where street lighting already lights the car sufficiently, no lighting of your own is required at all, which is why most parked cars in Berlin sit there completely dark and perfectly legally. What you may never do is *drive* on position lights alone: they mark a parked car, but they do not illuminate a road.

questions.text: How do you notice that your car has started to aquaplane?

options.text: The steering suddenly feels light, vague and spongy
The engine revs rise and you hear loud splashing from the wheel arches
The steering becomes noticeably heavy and stiff

questions.explanation: In aquaplaning the tyre can no longer push the water aside and rides up onto a wedge of water, losing contact with the road. Because the front tyres are no longer gripping, the steering goes eerily light and gives you no feedback at all, the opposite of heavy. The driven wheels spin up, so the engine note rises, and the water being slapped around inside the wheel arches gets loud. Those cues together are your warning that you are, briefly, a boat.

questions.text: Your car begins to aquaplane on a flooded stretch of road. What do you do?

options.text: Take your foot off the accelerator and hold the steering wheel straight
Avoid abrupt steering movements and heavy braking until the tyres grip again
Brake hard at once to get grip back as quickly as possible

questions.explanation: While the tyres are floating, nothing you ask of them arrives, but it is not discarded either. Steering input and brake pressure applied during aquaplaning are delivered all at once the instant the tyres touch down, which is how cars end up sideways. So do the boring thing: lift off the accelerator, keep the wheel straight, declutch or select N if you need to lose speed, and wait it out. Then reduce speed properly before the next patch of standing water, because prevention is the only reliable cure.

questions.text: A general danger sign warns you on a damp November morning at around 0 °C. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Bridges, shaded stretches and roads through woodland tend to freeze before the rest of the road
Wet leaves act like a lubricant and can rob you of grip
Black ice can only form once the thermometer reads below −5 °C

questions.explanation: Black ice does not wait for a deep freeze: a road surface chilled below zero plus rain, drizzle or thawing moisture is enough, so it commonly appears with the air temperature hovering around 0 °C, especially at dawn. It is also patchy. Bridges lose heat from underneath as well as on top, and shaded cuttings or wooded stretches get no sun, so those spots ice up first and thaw last while the rest of the road is merely wet. Wet leaves, wet cobbles and wet tram rails behave much the same way, with a slippery film hiding the surface beneath. The general danger sign (Gefahrstelle) is telling you something here needs attention: slow down and be ready to brake gently.

questions.text: What is the legally required minimum tread depth for car tyres in Germany, in millimetres?
questions.explanation: The legal minimum tread depth is 1.6 mm, measured in the main grooves of the tread. Legal is not the same as safe, though: tread is what pumps water out from under the tyre, so wet braking distances and aquaplaning resistance deteriorate sharply long before you reach that limit. Tyre experts therefore recommend replacing summer tyres from around 3 mm and winter tyres from around 4 mm.

questions.text: A deer steps onto the road in front of you on an unlit rural road. How do you react?

options.text: Brake hard, hold the steering wheel firmly and stay in your lane
Switch off the high beam so the animal is not transfixed by the light, and sound the horn
Swerve around the animal, even if that means crossing onto the oncoming lane

questions.explanation: Braking in a straight line is usually survivable; swerving frequently is not, because it sends you into oncoming traffic, a ditch or a tree. So brake as hard as the traffic behind you allows, grip the wheel with both hands to keep the car straight under heavy braking, and stay in your lane. Kill the high beam: bright light dazzles and freezes the animal so it stands there instead of moving off, whereas dipped beam plus the horn gives it a chance to clear. And expect more, because deer move in groups, so an apparently empty road after the first one means nothing.

questions.text: Which behaviours reduce your risk when driving at night or into low sun?

options.text: If an oncoming driver fails to dip, look towards the right-hand edge of your own lane and slow down instead of staring into the light
Keep the windscreen clean and the wipers and washers working, because low sun on dirty glass can hide a pedestrian completely
Wear sunglasses at night to cut the glare from oncoming headlights

questions.explanation: Glare works by overwhelming your eyes, so the cure is to stop looking at the source: shift your gaze to the right-hand edge of your lane, use it to hold your line, and take speed off until the other vehicle has passed. Never retaliate with your own high beam.  Keeping your view clear is also a legal duty, because a smeared windscreen turns low winter sun into an opaque white wall in which a pedestrian simply vanishes. Sunglasses at night are actively dangerous: they dim everything, including the dark-clothed cyclist you were supposed to spot, and they do nothing about the dazzle itself.
